_about.adopt_is_swift_only: The `order` section is `ThreadKeyring.wins`, and there is no Python implementation of it to check: `retired` is READ-ONLY on that side by design — the writer is the courier, which is Swift, and the machine never mints or destroys the memory key at all (§11.2). So Python asserts the documented rule rather than a function of its own: the winner is min(a, b) over the raw bytes, which is what `numerically smaller wins` means and what Python's own byte comparison does. That is an independent statement of the rule, not a call into moeledger, and it is why changing Swift's order and regenerating this file fails the Python suite. Python also checks the reachable consequence: the current key of every written vector is the winner of its pair.
_about.bytes: every key is 32 raw bytes as standard base64 with padding. The key material is fixed and legible on purpose — the leading byte decides every ordering question in this file, so a reader can check it by eye.
_about.duplicates: openingKeys must never name one key twice, and neither side leans on the writer for that: both deduplicate when they read (`ThreadKeyring.openingKeys`, `Keyring.opening_keys`). A repeat does reach the disk — `install` is `.callerWins` with no order test, so a key can be put back as current and displaced a second time — and `a-key-that-came-back-and-was-displaced-twice` is that file, retired list and all. It is the vector that makes the agreement checkable rather than asserted: two entries on disk, one key in the answer, on both sides.
_about.malformed_granularity: Swift parses `retired` as one cast of the whole field and Python element by element, so a file whose retired list mixes decodable keys with a non-string would lose ALL history on the Swift side and only that element on the Python side. Both still read the keyring, which is what §15.1 requires; the corpus keeps such a file to one thread so it does not pin a difference no writer can produce.
_about.refusal_is_spelled_differently: In `refused` the two sides express the same answer in their own idiom — Swift hands out no key (a fresh ThreadKeyring reads nothing and openingKeys is empty), Python raises VaultError. What the vector pins is that neither hands out a key and neither writes over the file.
_about.sealed: `sealed` carries ciphertext, so it is verified by opening, never compared: CryptoKit's nonce cannot be injected. Regeneration keeps a sample that still opens.
_about.text: `text` is the file byte for byte, in Foundation's [.prettyPrinted, .sortedKeys] form with no trailing newline. Python's moeledger.records.foundation_pretty_json reproduces it exactly; Keyring._write_keys then appends one newline, so a file Python has rewritten is this text plus \n and nothing else.
_about.what: CLOUD-PLAN §15.1's retired keys, pinned across the two implementations of thread-keys.json: Swift's ThreadKeyring, and Python's moeledger.vault.Keyring and claimstore.store.

order.name: differs-only-in-the-last-byte
order.why: Thirty-one identical bytes. A comparison that looked at the first byte alone would find no difference and call it a tie.

order.name: differs-only-in-the-last-byte-00-vs-ff
order.why: The same case at the ends of the byte range.

order.name: differs-only-in-the-first-byte
order.why: `a` is larger in every byte but the first, and wins on the first. The first byte that differs decides; nothing sums or averages.

order.name: differs-in-the-middle-and-contradicted-after
order.why: The bytes after the first difference point the other way, so a rule that let a later byte have the last word would get this wrong.

order.name: unsigned-not-signed
order.why: 0x7F against 0x80. Compared as signed bytes 0x80 is -128 and would win, which is the whole of the bug this pins.

order.name: the-two-keys-in-the-written-vectors
order.why: The tenant's key against the one this Mac minted while free. The written section is this pair's answer, on disk.

order.name: the-same-key-twice
order.why: Neither displaces the other, which is why re-delivering a key the courier already delivered retires nothing.

refused.name: the-file-is-not-an-object
refused.why: Not a keyring at all. Reading it as empty would replace it.

refused.name: keys-is-a-list
refused.why: The one field neither side may guess at.

refused.name: keys-is-missing-but-retired-is-not
refused.why: A file carrying history and no keys is not a keyring this build can write over, however well it understands the new field.

tolerated.name: retired-is-a-string
tolerated.why: A later build wrote something else under this name entirely.

tolerated.name: retired-is-a-list
tolerated.why: The same field as a list rather than a map of thread to keys.

tolerated.name: retired-maps-a-thread-to-a-string
tolerated.why: The field is the right shape and one thread's value is not.

tolerated.name: retired-is-an-empty-map
tolerated.why: A writer that emitted the field even with nothing to put in it.

tolerated.name: retired-holds-a-good-key-and-junk-beside-it
tolerated.why: One decodable key among entries that are not base64 and not 32 bytes. The good one survives; the rest are dropped rather than taking the keyring down with them.

tolerated.name: retired-holds-nothing-this-build-can-decode
tolerated.why: Both sides read this as no history, by different routes: Swift's cast of the whole field fails on the number, Python drops the two entries one at a time. The corpus keeps such a file to ONE thread deliberately — see _about.malformed_granularity.

written.name: a-free-mac-that-joined-a-tenant

sealed.text: the car is due in March

written.story: §15.1 itself: this Mac minted moe:memory while it ran free, then joined a tenant whose key wins the order. The tenant's key becomes the one everything seals under and the Mac's own is kept openable.

written.name: the-same-key-delivered-again-and-again
written.story: The courier ships every key it holds on every full run, so the tenant's key arrives over and over. Re-delivery must not fill the file with copies of one key.

written.name: a-key-that-came-back-and-was-displaced-twice
written.story: An enrolment installs the free Mac's own key over the tenant's — install is an instruction, and it does not retire anything — and the courier then displaces it a second time. The history on disk names that key TWICE, and both implementations still hand out each key once: the deduplication is on the read, where it is one rule rather than a promise every writer has to keep. This is the only vector whose file carries a repeat, and it is what makes that agreement checkable.

written.name: a-mac-displaced-twice-by-two-different-keys
written.story: Two displacements by two different keys. The order of the retired list is the order this Mac met them, oldest first — it is an array on disk and nothing sorts it.

written.name: a-keyring-from-before-15.1
written.story: Nothing was ever displaced, so the file carries no `retired` field at all and is byte-identical to one written before §15.1 existed. Every keyring on every Mac looks like this until the day it joins.
